idiom_name: ordinary initialize: assign the ivars, then call super(payload)
implementation_notes: Ruby's initializer is an ordinary method invoked by Class#new, and super re-invokes the same method in the superclass: the documentation states that super may be called as many times as you like in the subclass method, that bare super forwards the method's own arguments, that super() sends none and that explicit arguments such as super(@buf) send exactly those. Initialisation order is therefore whatever the method body says - build the payload into an instance variable first, then hand it to the superclass: @buf = Buffer.for_fd(fd); super(@buf). No helper class is needed, because a Ruby 'base' is just the next class in the ancestor chain whose initializer runs when you call it; the pattern's structural trick has no counterpart and no purpose here.
pitfalls: Bare super forwards the subclass method's arguments, so after a signature change it can hand the wrong payload to the superclass initializer; be explicit (super(@buf), or super() to forward nothing).

Nothing enforces the order: calling super first leaves the base holding nil, and with modules mixed into the ancestor chain it may be a module's initialize that runs before the class's - so the method that consumes the payload is decided by the ancestors list, not by the source layout.

Instance variables spring into existence on first assignment, so a wrong order does not raise where the mistake is: the base stores nil and the failure surfaces later at the first real use of the buffer.
